sections.html:
Lawrence is a compact city in Essex County, straddling the Merrimack River about 30 miles north-northwest of Boston. Its 89,143 residents (2020 census) share just 7.4 square miles, which works out to roughly 12,864 people per square mile. Methuen lies to the north, North Andover to the east and Andover to the south and southwest. Lawrence is also one of Essex County's two county seats, alongside Salem, so the district and superior courts sit here.

Four ZIP codes cover the city: 01840, 01841, 01842 and 01843.

The Essex Company began the Great Stone Dam in 1845, Lawrence became a town in 1847, and it was chartered as a city in 1853. Canals fed the mills, and workers arrived from Ireland, Germany, Sweden and French Canada, then from Italy and Eastern Europe. The nickname Immigrant City stuck.

Housing grew up around those mills: historic rowhouses and mill-era buildings packed into a small footprint. Many properties are older and hold more than one unit, so a seller here is often handling a multi-unit building rather than a single house. Age, wiring and heating systems drive most buyer questions.

Lawrence uses six council districts, and residents also place themselves by landmark.

  • Downtown and the canals: the North Canal, Great Stone Dam and mill buildings such as the Ayer Mills clock tower.
  • South Lawrence: the Shawsheen Fields area, where the first settlement in the present city began in 1655.
  • Tower Hill: high ground in the northwest, home to the 1895 High Service Water Tower.
  • Prospect Hill and Mount Vernon: hills on the northeastern and southern edges.
  • Den Rock Park: a wooded conservation area on the southern line shared with Andover.

When you describe a property to a buyer, name the area and the nearest landmark.

Interstate 495 crosses the eastern part of the city with three exits inside the limits. Route 28 runs north to south, Route 110 crosses the northern half, and Route 114 ends at Route 28 by the river. Lawrence is the western hub for Merrimack Valley Regional Transit Authority buses and has a stop on the MBTA Haverhill Line to North Station.

With highway, bus and commuter rail in one small city, buyers who work elsewhere in the region may consider a Lawrence house. Mention nearby transit in your description.

Real estate bills go out quarterly, on the first business day of July, October, January and April. Payment is due the first business day of August, November, February and May. Rates change each year, and you can estimate a bill by multiplying assessed value by the rate per $1,000.

The Treasurer/Collector's page on cityoflawrence.com also offers a tax bill lookup.

File an abatement application with the Assessor on the approved form. It has to reach the assessors by the due date of the first installment of the actual bill, usually February 1 where bills are quarterly. The assessors then have three months to answer before the application is treated as denied.

You also need to have paid every installment on time. Check the details on your own bill and phone the Assessor before the deadline. If you plan to sell within weeks, an appeal will probably not finish first, so weigh whether it is worth the effort.

On September 13, 2018, a series of gas explosions and fires hit as many as 40 homes across Lawrence, Andover and North Andover. One resident died, and more than 30,000 customers left their homes. A second leak a year later, on September 27, 2019, again forced evacuations.

Some buyers still ask about a home's heating system, the gas service and its age. Keep records of any boiler, furnace or gas line work, and hand the paperwork over early. A cash buyer will usually inspect the system in person anyway.

An attorney handles title and closing work. Massachusetts keeps two title systems: recorded land, filed with the Registry of Deeds, and registered land, filed through the Land Court.

Two state items catch many sellers off guard.

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. The fire department inspects alarms and issues a certificate of compliance. Book it as soon as a closing date is set.
  • Home inspection waivers. State rule 760 CMR 74 limits sellers of certain residential properties from conditioning offers on a buyer's waiver of inspection.

Deed excise is $2 per $500 of consideration and is usually paid by the seller. Ask the Essex County registry for the current total before you sign.

sections.h2: Selling a multi-family or inherited property
sections.html:
Older and multi-unit housing creates a few situations that come up again and again.

  • An inherited two- or three-family house with tenants and no one to manage it.
  • Roof, porch or heating repairs that cost more than the owner can fund.
  • Unpaid taxes or water charges that need a payoff.
  • A house on a small lot, which can narrow the pool of conventional buyers.

If you ask for a cash offer, we look at the building as it is and tell you what we would pay. Set that number against repair costs and the time a listing would take.

A cash buyer does not need a lender, so there is no appraisal ordered by a bank, no loan commitment to wait on and no financing contingency that can collapse a week before closing. Showings are limited to a visit or two, and you are not asked to repaint, patch a roof or clear out every room first.

Everything required by Massachusetts still applies. The alarm certificate, title search, payoff letters and deed recording all happen, and your attorney still reviews the purchase and sale agreement. What changes is the number of parties who can delay you.

sections.h2: What to line up before closing
sections.html:
Collect the current tax bill, any water balance, mortgage payoff statements and tenant lease copies if units are rented. Ask the Collector whether anything is overdue, because unpaid balances get settled from your proceeds. Book the fire department visit early, since a failed alarm check is a fixable delay only if you leave time to fix it.

If the house came through an estate, the attorney will also want the papers showing who may sign the deed. Having all of this in one folder shortens the path from accepted offer to funds in your account, and it lets a buyer's attorney answer title questions without sending you back to the office for another copy.

faqs.q: When are Lawrence property tax bills due?
faqs.a: Real estate bills are due on the first business day of August, November, February and May. They are issued on the first business day of July, October, January and April.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Lawrence assessed value?
faqs.a: Call the Lawrence Assessor at (978) 620-3190. For overdue balances or tax title accounts, the Collector's office takes calls at (978) 620-3170.

faqs.q: Is a smoke detector inspection required to sell in Lawrence?
faqs.a: Yes. Massachusetts requires a fire department certificate of compliance when a home is sold or transferred. Contact the department to schedule the visit and ask about the fee.
Lawrence is in Essex County, Massachusetts, one of two county seats along with Salem. Deeds for Lawrence properties are recorded through the Essex County registry system.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lawrence multi-family house as-is?
faqs.a: Yes. You can sell the building in its current condition. Expect the buyer to review the units, tenants and systems, and plan for the fire department certificate and any tax payoff.
